title: Marmalade loaf cake
subtitle: Orange marmalade loaf with a sticky glazed top
excerpt: Marmalade loaf cake folds good orange marmalade into a simple butter sponge, giving a bitter-sweet flavour with small flecks of peel throughout. It keeps well for three to four days, improving in texture as the marmalade settles. Use a thin-cut marmalade for the best distribution through the batter.
sourceNotes: British loaf cake tradition documented in various 20th-century household baking manuals (public domain). Constance Spry (The Constance Spry Cookery Book, 1956, public domain). Mrs Beeton (Book of Household Management, 1861, public domain).

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap unglazed in foil and freeze for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten the day after baking when the marmalade has settled into the crumb.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 160 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 145 degrees Celsius. Bake on the middle shelf.
baking.decoratingTechnique: Warm marmalade glaze brushed over while hot

glossaryTerms.definition: Beating softened butter and sugar together until the mixture is pale, light, and fluffy before adding eggs and flour. The process incorporates air into the fat, which helps the cake rise. The butter must be genuinely soft, not melted, for the method to work.

A pourable or spoonable raw cake or bread mixture containing flour, liquid, and usually eggs and fat. Cake batters range from thin and pourable to thick and spoonable. A loaf cake batter sits at the thicker end and holds its shape when spooned into the tin.

content.text: to produce a light, open crumb that carries the marmalade well. The
is thick but should drop from the spoon with a firm shake. The glaze goes on while the cake is still hot so it soaks in slightly and sets to a sticky finish.

Heat the oven to 160 degrees Celsius (conventional) or 145 degrees Celsius (fan). Grease a 900 g (2 lb) loaf tin and line with a strip of baking paper that covers the base and both long sides, leaving an overhang to use as handles.
Beat the butter and caster sugar together in a large bowl until very pale and fluffy, about 4 minutes with a hand mixer. Scrape down the sides of the bowl halfway through.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each. If the mixture begins to look curdled, add a spoonful of the flour. Beat in the orange zest and the marmalade.
Fold in the self-raising flour with a large silicone spatula, then fold in the milk to loosen the batter slightly. Spoon into the lined loaf tin and level the top.

Bake on the middle shelf for 50 to 55 minutes until the cake is deep golden brown, has risen well, and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. The top will crack along the centre; this is correct.

While the cake is still in the tin and hot from the oven, make the glaze: warm the marmalade in a small saucepan over low heat until loosened, stir in the icing sugar, and brush all over the top surface. Leave in the tin for 10 minutes, then lift out using the paper handles and cool on a rack.

attrs.avoid: Avoid adding cold eggs straight from the refrigerator.
attrs.fix: Use eggs at room temperature and add them slowly. If the mixture does split, stir in a tablespoon of flour before continuing. The finished cake will not be affected.

attrs.problem: Cake sinks in the centre after baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid opening the oven door before 40 minutes.
attrs.fix: A sunken centre usually means the bake was cut short. Check with a skewer before removing; if it comes out with wet batter, return to the oven for a further 5 to 10 minutes.

attrs.problem: Marmalade peel clumps in one area
attrs.avoid: Avoid using a thick-cut marmalade for this cake.
attrs.fix: Thin-cut marmalade distributes more evenly through the batter. If only thick-cut is available, roughly chop the peel strips before measuring.
